holidays.name: Tell a Fairy Tale Day
holidays.description: Dust off your favorite once-upon-a-time and tell it out loud. Do it with dramatic voices, a wicked witch cackle, and a happily-ever-after finish. Kids, grandparents, and coworkers on a lunch break all make fine audiences.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance of unclear origin. It encourages the old art of oral storytelling, which long predates printed books.
holidays.funFact: Many classic fairy tales were passed along by word of mouth for generations before anyone wrote them down. Early versions were often much darker than the ones told at bedtime today.

holidays.name: National Pistachio Day
holidays.description: This is a day for cracking open the world's most satisfyingly snackable green nut. Eat them straight from the shell, bake them into baklava, or stir them into ice cream. Then admire the pile of empty shells you've made.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial food observance of unclear origin. Nut lovers claim it every February 26.
holidays.funFact: Pistachios are technically seeds of a fruit and belong to the same plant family as cashews and mangoes. Their shells split open on their own as the seeds ripen, which is why they look like they're smiling.

holidays.name: Thermos Bottle Day
holidays.description: Raise a steaming cup to the humble vacuum flask. It keeps your cocoa hot and your lemonade cold, and it has been doing so for over a century. Pack a thermos for a picnic or a snowy walk today.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance honoring the vacuum-insulated bottle. Scottish scientist James Dewar invented the underlying technology in the 1890s, and German glassblowers later turned it into a household product.
holidays.funFact: 'Thermos' started out as a brand name, taken from the Greek word for 'hot.' It became so widely used that courts eventually treated it as a generic term for vacuum flasks in the United States.
